# rapidoc validate

> Check an OpenAPI spec strictly against the specification, with file, line and column for each error, in CI too.

```bash
npx rapidoc validate openapi.yaml
npx rapidoc validate https://example.com/openapi.json
npx rapidoc validate                       # in a portal: every local OpenAPI spec in apis:, and the Arazzo specs
```

`rapidoc validate` checks an OpenAPI spec strictly against the OpenAPI Specification (2.0, 3.0, 3.1 and 3.2):

- **Required fields and types**, as the specification's schema for that version defines them: `info.version`, a response's `description`, `type` values, and so on.
- **Path parameters**: every `{name}` in a path must be defined as a `path` parameter, on the path or on each operation (a `$ref` to a parameter counts).
- **`$ref`s**: each must point to something. Files reached through a relative `$ref` are checked too.

Each error names the file, line and column, and the JSON pointer of what's wrong; an error inside a file reached through `$ref` points into that file:

```text
🔍 orders: specs/orders.yaml
   ❌ 2 error(s):
      specs/orders.yaml:3:1  must have required property 'version'  (#/info)
      specs/shared/responses.yaml:12:3  must have required property 'description'  (#/NotFound)
```

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `--format pretty \| json \| sarif` | `pretty` (default) for the terminal; `json` for scripts; `sarif` for GitHub code scanning. `json` and `sarif` print one document on stdout and nothing else. |
| `--strict` | Fail on warnings too. |
| `--remote` | Also fetch and check remote `$ref`s (and, in a portal, remote specs in `apis:`). Without it they are skipped, with a warning for `$ref`s. A spec given as a URL is always fetched. |

## In CI

It exits with code `1` when the spec has errors (or warnings, with `--strict`), so it can gate a pull request:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/api.yml"
# in a job's steps:
- run: npx rapidoc validate openapi.yaml
```

To see the problems on the pull request itself, upload a SARIF report to GitHub code scanning:

```yaml title=".github/workflows/api.yml"
permissions:
  security-events: write
# in a job's steps:
- run: npx rapidoc validate openapi.yaml --format sarif > rapidoc.sarif || true
- uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
  with:
    sarif_file: rapidoc.sarif
```

## In a portal

Run without a file in a [RapiDoc Portal](https://portal.rapidocui.com/) folder, it validates every local OpenAPI spec in `apis:` and the Arazzo specs. With `@rapidoc/portal` installed it also warns about operations without an `operationId` (their page URLs change when their summary is edited), and checks that each workflow's steps resolve against your APIs.

Validating one file needs only `@rapidoc/cli`; validating a whole portal reads its config, so it needs `@rapidoc/portal`.

To check what makes a good reference beyond validity (summaries, examples, operationIds), use [`rapidoc lint`](/docs/cli/lint/), which runs this check first.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/cli/validate/

---

# MCP Server

> How RapiDoc turns an OpenAPI spec into a curated Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for AI agents - which operations become tools, and the manifest.

AI agents such as Claude and Cursor call APIs through tools served over the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**. RapiDoc turns your OpenAPI spec into an MCP server, and curates it on the way, because exposing every endpoint one-to-one works poorly for agents: internal endpoints leak, transport headers become tool arguments the model has to guess, and every extra tool costs context on every turn.

RapiDoc reads your plain OpenAPI spec, leaves out internal and deprecated operations, strips transport and credential headers from tool arguments, and turns reference-data lookups into MCP resources. The result is an **MCP manifest**: plain JSON with one tool per operation, real JSON Schema arguments and MCP safety annotations. It ships in a small TypeScript project you can run as-is.

You can create it three ways:

- **In the browser**: the **Export MCP Server** button of `<rapi-doc>` (or its JavaScript methods), described with [RapiDoc](/docs/rapidoc/mcp-export/). Nothing is sent to a server.
- **On the command line**: `rapidoc mcp export` and `rapidoc mcp serve` (`@rapidoc/cli`).
- **In Node**: `@rapidoc/mcp`, for build scripts and your own servers.

> **Tip:**
> The [MCP Server example](/examples/mcp-server) shows the manifest, server and runtime for a real OpenAPI spec.
>
>   The export runs in the browser and sends nothing anywhere. You unzip and install the project on your machine, and your AI app starts it as a child process that talks over stdin and stdout, on no port.

## How operations become tools

No extra annotations are needed. Every tool and resource comes from standard OpenAPI fields:

1. **Tool names**: The tool name is the snake_case form of the `operationId` (`placeOrder` becomes `place_order`). Operations without an `operationId` get a name derived from the HTTP method and path. Duplicate names get a `_2`, `_3` suffix.
2. **Tool descriptions**: The operation `summary` is used, else its `description`, else `METHOD /path`. HTML and Markdown are stripped and the text is truncated to 300 characters.
3. **Left out**: Operations marked `x-internal: true` or `x-hidden: true`, operations marked `deprecated: true`, and webhooks are left out.
4. **Headers**: Headers like `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `X-Api-Key`, `Accept`, `User-Agent` and other transport metadata are stripped from LLM tool arguments, as is any parameter that carries an API key named in the spec's `securitySchemes`. A secret passed in a parameter the spec does not declare as a security scheme stays an argument, so declare it. The runtime applies the right scheme itself, from environment variables, and reads the base URL from `servers[0]`. The exported server runs outside the documentation page, so it needs a full URL: when the spec has no `servers`, or a relative one such as `/api/v1`, set `API_BASE_URL`, which also overrides a full URL.
5. **Resources**: A `GET` with no required parameters whose path contains a reference-data word (`/reference`, `/currencies`, `/countries`, `/tiers`, `/categories`, `/schema`) becomes an **MCP resource** instead of a tool. Many hosts leave resources for the user to attach, so set `x-mcp-resource: false` on an operation the agent must be able to call itself; `x-mcp-resource: true` makes any `GET` with no required parameters a resource. Its URI is `reference://` and the tool name without `get_`, with dashes (`getCurrencies` becomes `reference://currencies`).
6. **Safety annotations**: Every tool carries MCP annotations: `readOnlyHint` for `GET` only, `idempotentHint` for `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE`, and `destructiveHint`: `true` for `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE`, `false` for `GET`, and left out for `POST`, which may add (`POST /orders`) or undo (`POST /orders/{id}/cancel`). Without the hint, hosts assume a tool may be destructive. Hosts use the annotations to ask the user before running a consequential tool; they are hints, not enforcement.
7. **Token budget**: RapiDoc estimates how many tokens the tool list adds to every turn, and warns above 30 tools or 5,000 tokens.

---

## Example

Here is a plain OpenAPI 3.x snippet and how each operation is treated:

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Commerce Fulfillment API
  version: 2.4.0
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com/v2   # Base URL in the manifest
security:
  - api_key: []                         # Applied by the runtime from API_KEY

paths:
  # 1. Tool "place_order" (POST: readOnlyHint false, no destructiveHint)
  /orders:
    post:
      summary: Place a new order
      operationId: placeOrder
      parameters:
        - name: Authorization # Stripped: never a tool argument
          in: header
          schema: { type: string }
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [customerId, items]
              properties:
                customerId: { type: string }
                items: { type: array, items: { type: string } }
                shippingMethod: { type: string, enum: [standard, express, overnight] }

  # 2. Read-only tool "get_order"
  /orders/{orderId}:
    get:
      summary: Get an order
      operationId: getOrder
      parameters:
        - name: orderId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: { type: string }

  # 3. MCP Resource "reference://currencies" (GET, no required params, reference-data path)
  /currencies:
    get:
      summary: List supported currencies
      operationId: getCurrencies

  # 4. Excluded: internal endpoint
  /admin/database/vacuum:
    post:
      summary: Trigger internal database maintenance
      x-internal: true

  # 5. Excluded: deprecated endpoint
  /orders/legacy:
    get:
      summary: Legacy order list
      deprecated: true

components:
  securitySchemes:
    api_key:
      type: apiKey
      in: header
      name: X-API-Key
```

---

## The Manifest

The export is data, not generated code. `manifest.json` describes the whole server:

- **`server`**: `name` (snake_case of the `mcp-server-name` attribute or the API title), `version` and `description` from `info`.
- **`sources`**: the API, named `api`, with the `baseUrl` from `servers[0]` (server variables filled with their defaults) and the OpenAPI spec's `securitySchemes` copied as they are. An Arazzo spec can add more sources.
- **`tools`**: one per operation that survives the exclusions above.
- **`resources`**: the reference-data lookups, with a `reference://` URI.
- **`workflows`**: one entry per Arazzo workflow when an Arazzo spec is given (see [Workflows as tools](#workflows-as-tools)); otherwise empty.

Each tool has a `name`, a `description`, an `inputSchema`, MCP `annotations` and an `operation` block that tells the runtime how to make the HTTP call. The `inputSchema` is real JSON Schema: path, query, header and cookie parameters become properties by name, and the request body becomes a `body` property holding the full body schema, with nested objects, arrays, enums and `required` intact. `$ref`s are inlined, cycles are cut, and read-only properties are dropped because they never go in a request.

The `place_order` tool from the example above:

```json
{
  "name": "place_order",
  "description": "Place a new order",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "body": {
        "type": "object",
        "required": ["customerId", "items"],
        "properties": {
          "customerId": { "type": "string" },
          "items": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } },
          "shippingMethod": { "type": "string", "enum": ["standard", "express", "overnight"] }
        }
      }
    },
    "required": ["body"]
  },
  "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": false, "idempotentHint": false },
  "operation": {
    "source": "api",
    "method": "POST",
    "path": "/orders",
    "params": [{ "name": "body", "in": "body", "contentType": "application/json" }],
    "security": [{ "api_key": [] }]
  }
}
```

`operation.params` records where each argument goes (`path`, `query`, `header`, `cookie` or `body`), and `operation.security` is the operation's security requirement, else the OpenAPI spec's. Only a TypeScript server is exported today. Because the manifest holds everything a server needs, a server in another language would only have to read the same `manifest.json`; nothing would need to be regenerated.

## Next

[Export and run the server](/docs/mcp/server/): the runtime, the exported project, creating it from `<rapi-doc>`, the command line or Node, and connecting an AI app.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/mcp/

---

# Export and Run the Server

> Create the MCP server from <rapi-doc>, the command line or Node, what the exported project holds, how it runs, and how to connect an AI app to it.

The [manifest](/docs/mcp/#the-manifest) ships in a small TypeScript project you can run as it is. This page covers the runtime and the project, the ways to create them, and how an AI app starts the server.

## The Runtime and the Exported Project

### The runtime

`runtime.js` executes any tool in the manifest with `fetch`, so the same file runs in Node, browsers and edge workers. `createMcpRuntime(manifest, { fetch, credentials, baseUrls })` returns `listTools()`, `listResources()`, `callTool(name, args)` and `readResource(uri)`. A tool call:

1. Puts each argument where `operation.params` says, percent-encoding path parameters and serializing arrays as repeated query parameters. A path argument of `.` or `..` is an error, because a URL would resolve it to another path.
2. Applies the security scheme: an API key in a header, query parameter or cookie; HTTP Basic; a Bearer token for HTTP bearer, OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect. For OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect you supply an access token you already have: the runtime does not sign in or refresh a token.
3. Sends the request and returns an MCP result: `content` with the JSON response pretty-printed, `structuredContent` when the response is a JSON object, and `isError` with the HTTP status and body on a 4xx or 5xx.

### What is in the zip

**Export MCP Server** downloads `<server-name>-mcp.zip` (a server name that already ends in `-mcp` is not suffixed again):

| File | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `manifest.json` | The manifest described above |
| `runtime.js` | The runtime for operation tools; identical for every API |
| `workflow-runtime.js` | Runs workflow tools; present only when the manifest has workflows, identical for every API |
| `server.ts` | A stdio server on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` that registers the manifest's tools and resources and hands every call to the runtime; identical for every API |
| `package.json` | Depends on `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`; `tsx` as a dev dependency; `npm start` runs `tsx server.ts` |
| `README.md` | How to run it and which environment variables it reads |
| `mcp.json` | A ready-made `mcpServers` entry for Claude Desktop, Cursor and other MCP hosts |

### Running it

```bash
unzip commerce-fulfillment-api-mcp.zip -d commerce-fulfillment-api-mcp
cd commerce-fulfillment-api-mcp
npm install
API_KEY="your-key" npm start
```

When the server is up, `npm start` prints a line such as `[MCP] my_api: 2 tools on stdio`; stop it with Ctrl+C. It also starts without credentials, and calls then return the API's error. `server.ts` and the runtimes are the same for every API, so `manifest.json` is the one file to review.

### Environment variables

Credentials are read from environment variables named after the security schemes in the OpenAPI spec, in upper snake case: the scheme `petstore_auth` (or `petstoreAuth`) reads `PETSTORE_AUTH`, `api_key` reads `API_KEY`. The agent never sees or supplies a credential: the server adds it to each request. When the spec has one scheme, `API_KEY` also works as its variable; with several schemes, each needs its own variable, so one key is never sent as another scheme's credential. HTTP Basic takes `user:password` in the scheme's variable, or `<NAME>_USERNAME` and `<NAME>_PASSWORD`. `API_BASE_URL` overrides the manifest's base URL for every source. `EXTERNAL_HOSTS` (comma-separated, `*` for any) lists the hosts a workflow step's [`x-operation`](https://flow.rapidocui.com/docs/extensions/#calls-outside-the-api-sources-x-operation) URL computed at run time may go to, besides those the workflow names. `rapidoc mcp serve` and `rapidoc serve` read the same variable.

### Workflows as tools

When the page also has a [`<rapi-flow>`](https://flow.rapidocui.com/) element tied to the `<rapi-doc>` (or you pass `--arazzo` to `rapidoc mcp`), the export adds one tool per Arazzo workflow. The manifest's `workflows` holds each workflow's steps with their operations resolved, and the runtime runs them: inputs become the tool's arguments (one left out gets its `default` from the workflow's `inputs` schema), every step's parameters and body are filled from `$inputs` and earlier steps' outputs, success criteria are checked (a step without criteria succeeds on a 2xx response), `onSuccess` / `onFailure` actions (`end`, `goto`, `retry`) are followed, and the workflow's `outputs` are the result. The same runtime powers the **Run** button of `<rapi-flow>`, which runs a workflow in the browser with the credentials entered in the tied `<rapi-doc>` and lights up each step. A workflow that uses something the runtime does not run yet (a step that calls another workflow, `regex` / `jsonpath` / `xpath` criteria) is left out, and `generateMcpServer().problems` says why.

For a server with only the workflow tools, and no tool per operation, export from `<rapi-flow>` itself: with `mcp="true"` it shows its own **Export MCP Server** button (see [Workflows](https://flow.rapidocui.com/)). Its steps call every API source of the Arazzo spec, where `<rapi-doc>` knows one. A short list of task-sized tools is often easier for a model to use, and cheaper in tokens. From `<rapi-doc>`'s code, `downloadMcpServer({ includeOperations: false })` builds the same for its one API (`<server-name>-workflows-mcp.zip`).

```javascript
import { buildMcpManifest, createMcpRuntime, parseArazzo } from '@rapidoc/mcp';

const arazzo = parseArazzo(readFileSync('petstore.arazzo.yaml', 'utf8'));
const manifest = buildMcpManifest(spec, { arazzo, onProblem: console.warn });
const runtime = createMcpRuntime(manifest, { credentials: { api_key: process.env.API_KEY } });
const result = await runtime.callTool('adopt_pet', { quantity: 1 }, {
  onStep: (step) => console.log(step.stepId, step.outcome, step.response?.status),
});
```

## Creating the server

### In `<rapi-doc>`

The `mcp` attribute shows an **Export MCP Server** button that downloads the project as a zip, and the element's methods build the same in code. Both are on [Export MCP Server](/docs/rapidoc/mcp-export/) in RapiDoc's docs.

### From the command line

`npx rapidoc mcp export openapi.yaml` writes the same project as the Export button, and `npx rapidoc mcp serve openapi.yaml` runs the server over stdio without writing files ([Command Line](/docs/cli/mcp/)):

```bash
npx rapidoc mcp export my-api.yaml --out-dir my-api-mcp --server-name my-api
```

### In Node: `@rapidoc/mcp`

The same builder, runtime and project writer are available without the browser or any element, for build scripts and servers:

```bash
npm install @rapidoc/mcp
```

```javascript
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { parse } from 'yaml';
import { buildMcpManifest, createMcpRuntime, writeMcpProject } from '@rapidoc/mcp';

const spec = parse(readFileSync('openapi.yaml', 'utf8'));
const manifest = buildMcpManifest(spec, { serverName: 'petstore' });

// Call a tool directly, with credentials by security scheme
const runtime = createMcpRuntime(manifest, { credentials: { api_key: process.env.API_KEY } });
const result = await runtime.callTool('get_pet_by_id', { petId: 1 });

// Or write the same project the Export button downloads
const files = writeMcpProject(manifest); // path → text

// When you know where the project will live, put the real path in mcp.json
writeMcpProject(manifest, { serverPath: '/srv/petstore-mcp/server.ts' });
```

`@rapidoc/mcp` ships TypeScript types (`McpManifest`, `McpRuntime`, ...). Its only dependency is `yaml` (for Arazzo specs); requests use Node's `fetch`.

## Connecting an AI App

Every exported project includes `mcp.json`, a ready-to-use `mcpServers` entry. It is a template: nothing is added to your AI app until you copy it into the app's configuration. Any app that can start a local MCP server over stdio can use the server: **Claude Desktop**, **Cursor**, Claude Code, Codex and others. Most read this JSON format; an app with another format (Codex uses TOML) takes the same command, arguments and variables. The entry has one `env` entry per security scheme in the spec (`API_KEY` alone when the spec declares none).

Add the entry to the `mcpServers` object of the app's own configuration file, keeping the entries already there, and replace the placeholder path in `args` with the absolute path of the unzipped folder's `server.ts` (`rapidoc mcp export` writes the real path). Run `npm install` in that folder first. The app starts the server itself, as a child process that talks over stdin and stdout; it listens on no port, and `npm start` is only for trying it out.

| App | Configuration file |
| :--- | :--- |
| Claude Desktop, macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` |
| Claude Desktop, Windows | `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, or `.cursor/mcp.json` in a project |
| Claude Code | `.mcp.json` in a project |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml`: a `[mcp_servers.<name>]` section with the same `command`, `args` and `env`, written as TOML |

> **Caution:**
> Every tool call is a real request to your API, made with the credentials you set. Use a key with only the permissions the agent should have, or point `API_BASE_URL` at a staging server. Leaving an operation out of the export keeps it off the tool list; it is not access control.
>
>   - The safety annotations are hints for the AI app; the server has no confirmation step of its own.
>   - The OpenAPI spec's text and the API's responses reach the model as they are. Export only from specs you trust.
>   - The server talks over stdio, so it works with AI apps on your machine. A hosted or remote AI app can't reach it.

For the Swagger Petstore, which declares the schemes `api_key` and `petstore_auth`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "petstore_mcp": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "tsx", "/absolute/path/to/petstore-mcp/server.ts"],
      "env": {
        "API_KEY": "your-api-key",
        "PETSTORE_AUTH": "your-petstore-auth"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Restart the app after changing its configuration. If the tools don't appear, check that the path in `args` is absolute (the app starts the server from its own folder) and correct, and that `npm install` ran in the project; the app's MCP log shows why a server didn't start.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/mcp/server/

---

# Pre-rendering

> Render a RapiDoc API reference to HTML at build time with @rapidoc/prerender: Declarative Shadow DOM that shows before any JavaScript runs, and that search engines can read.

`<rapi-doc>` renders in the browser, so until its script runs the page is empty, and a crawler that doesn't run JavaScript sees nothing. `@rapidoc/prerender` renders the same templates at build time, in Node or Bun, and returns HTML: the reference shows on the first paint, and search engines index it. Load `rapidoc` in the page too, and the element takes over the pre-rendered markup for **Try**, search and navigation.

```bash
npm install @rapidoc/prerender
```

It needs Node 22.12 or later.

## Render the whole reference

`renderRapiDoc` returns a `<rapi-doc>` element with its content inside, as [Declarative Shadow DOM](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/template#shadowrootmode): the browser attaches the shadow root while parsing, before any script runs.

<Tabs syncKey="prerender">
  <TabItem label="Node or Bun">
```javascript title="prerender.mjs"
import fs from 'node:fs';
import { renderRapiDoc } from '@rapidoc/prerender';

const reference = await renderRapiDoc({
  spec: './specs/petstore.yaml', // a file, a URL, spec text or a spec object
  renderStyle: 'read',
  theme: 'ember',
  colorScheme: 'dark',
});

fs.writeFileSync('./dist/api.html', `<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>API Reference</title>
    <script type="module" src="https://unpkg.com/rapidoc/dist/rapidoc-min.js"></script>
  </head>
  <body>${reference}</body>
</html>`);
```
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Astro">
```astro title="src/pages/api.astro"
---
import { renderRapiDoc } from '@rapidoc/prerender';

const reference = await renderRapiDoc({ spec: './public/specs/petstore.json', renderStyle: 'read' });
---

<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <script type="module" src="https://unpkg.com/rapidoc/dist/rapidoc-min.js"></script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <Fragment set:html={reference} />
  </body>
</html>
```
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Next.js">
```tsx title="app/api-reference/page.tsx"
import { renderRapiDoc } from '@rapidoc/prerender';
import Script from 'next/script';

export default async function ApiReferencePage() {
  const reference = await renderRapiDoc({ spec: 'https://api.example.com/openapi.json' });

  return (
    <main>
      <Script type="module" src="https://unpkg.com/rapidoc/dist/rapidoc-min.js" />
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: reference }} />
    </main>
  );
}
```
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

The output looks like this:

```html
<rapi-doc theme="ember" color-scheme="dark" render-style="read" layout="column">
  <template shadowrootmode="open">
    <style>/* the element's styles */</style>
    <!-- navigation, tags, operations and schemas, as the element renders them -->
  </template>
</rapi-doc>
```

With `outputMode: 'html'` (or `'light'`) you get plain light-DOM HTML in a `<div class="rapidoc-prerender-container">` with scoped styles instead: static, with nothing for the element to take over.

## Render one endpoint or one schema

`renderEndpoint` and `renderSchema` render a single operation or schema, for a guide or a blog post built at build time. Their output is light-DOM HTML with its own styles, so it needs no JavaScript at all. This card was rendered when this site was built:

<PrerenderEndpointDemo />

```javascript
import { renderEndpoint, renderSchema } from '@rapidoc/prerender';

const endpoint = await renderEndpoint({
  spec: './specs/logistics.yaml',
  path: '/shipments/{shipmentId}',
  method: 'get',
  allowTry: false,
});

const schema = await renderSchema({
  spec: './specs/logistics.yaml',
  schema: 'ShipmentResponse', // a name under components/schemas, or a schema object
  style: 'table',             // or 'tree'
});
```

For an interactive single endpoint in the browser instead, use [`<rapi-doc-mini>`](/docs/rapidoc-mini/).

## Options

`renderRapiDoc` takes the attributes of `<rapi-doc>` in camelCase. The main ones:

| Option | Default | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `spec` | (required) | A file path, a URL, spec text (JSON or YAML) or a spec object. |
| `renderStyle` | `'read'` | `'read'`, `'view'` or `'focused'`. |
| `layout` | `'column'` for read and focused, `'row'` for view | Request and response side by side, or one above the other. |
| `theme` | `'amber'` | A preset (`ember`, `carbon`, `cobalt`, `jade`, `indigo`, `amber`) or a hex color. |
| `colorScheme` | `'dark'` | `'dark'`, `'light'` or `'system'`. |
| `schemaStyle` | `'table'` | `'table'` or `'tree'`. |
| `schemaExpandLevel` | `99999` | How many schema levels start expanded. |
| `defaultSchemaTab` | | `'example'` or `'schema'`. |
| `filterOperations` | | Which operations to render, as [`filter-operations`](/docs/rapidoc/reference/#filter-operations). |
| `showHeader`, `showSideNav`, `showInfo` | | Show or hide those parts, as on the element. |
| `allowTry`, `allowSearch`, `allowAdvancedSearch`, `allowServerSelection`, `allowAuthentication` | | Include those features, as on the element. |
| `focusedElementId` | `'overview'` | The operation shown first in focused mode. |
| `pageDirection` | | `'ltr'` or `'rtl'`. |
| `outputMode` | `'dsd'` | `'dsd'` (Declarative Shadow DOM), or `'html'` / `'light'` for plain light-DOM HTML. |
| `includeStyles` | `true` | Inline the element's styles in the output. |
| `inlineSpec` | `true` | With a spec object, inline it in the output, so the element doesn't fetch it again. |

`renderEndpoint` takes `spec`, `path`, `method`, and `renderStyle`, `layout`, `theme`, `colorScheme`, `includeStyles`, `allowTry` and `schemaStyle`. `renderSchema` takes `schema`, `spec`, `style`, `schemaExpandLevel`, `theme`, `colorScheme` and `includeStyles`. The types are in the package's `index.d.ts`.

## A static sidebar

For a site that draws its own navigation beside a headless `<rapi-doc>`, as the [RapiDoc Portal](https://portal.rapidocui.com/) does, the package also renders the sidebar: `getNavBarHtml(spec, options)` returns its HTML, `getNavCss()` and `getThemeTokensCss(theme)` its styles, and `bindNavBar(sidebar, rapiDoc)` ties it to the element in the browser, so clicks scroll the reference and the current operation is highlighted. `getSpecNavigation(spec)` returns the same tags and operations as data, to build your own. Its options follow `<rapi-doc>`'s sidebar attributes: `showMethodInNavBar`, `usePathInNav` and `showBadgesInNavBar` (`"dot"`, the default, marks items whose operation shows a badge; `"false"` turns that off).

> **Note:**
> The pre-rendered HTML comes from the same templates as the element, so the two match.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/prerender/

---

# Integrations

> Which RapiDoc integration to use for your front-end framework, server framework or documentation site.

`<rapi-doc>` is a standard custom element, so a page in any framework can use it with a line of setup. The integrations go further: they serve the reference from the app that serves your API, or add reference pages to your documentation site, so there is no HTML to write.

| You have | Use | Page |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| A React, Next.js, Vue, Nuxt, Angular, Svelte or Astro app | `rapidoc`, the element itself | [Front-End Frameworks](/docs/integrations/front-end/) |
| A Hono, Express or Fastify API | `@rapidoc/hono`, `@rapidoc/express`, `@rapidoc/fastify` | [Hono, Express & Fastify](/docs/integrations/node/) |
| A FastAPI or Starlette API | `rapidoc` on PyPI | [FastAPI & Starlette](/docs/integrations/python/) |
| An ASP.NET Core API | `RapiDoc.AspNetCore` on NuGet | [ASP.NET Core](/docs/integrations/dotnet/) |
| A Go API (`net/http`, chi, Gin, Echo, Fiber) | `github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go` | [Go](/docs/integrations/go/) |
| A Starlight, VitePress or Docusaurus site | `@rapidoc/starlight`, `@rapidoc/vitepress`, `@rapidoc/docusaurus` | [Documentation Sites](/docs/integrations/docs-sites/) |
| A full developer portal, with guides, search and sign-in | `@rapidoc/cli` and `@rapidoc/portal` | [RapiDoc Portal](https://portal.rapidocui.com/) |

## One contract

The server-framework packages all follow one contract, defined in `@rapidoc/embed`: they take the same options (any attribute of `<rapi-doc>`), serve the same routes (the page at `/docs`, the bundle, the OAuth return page) and send the same HTML. The Python, .NET and Go packages are ports of it that pass the same fixtures. So moving an API from one framework to another keeps its reference the same.

<CardGrid>
  <LinkCard title="Build an Integration" href="/docs/integrations/build-your-own/" description="Write one for another framework, site generator or tool, in any language." />
  <LinkCard title="All integrations at a glance" href="/integrations/" description="The overview page, with the install line of each." />
</CardGrid>

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/

---

# Build an Integration

> Write a RapiDoc plugin for a web framework, a documentation site or another tool, in any language.

An integration adds a `<rapi-doc>` API reference to something else: a web framework (Hono, FastAPI, Spring Boot, ASP.NET Core), a documentation site (Starlight, VitePress) or a tool (VS Code, Confluence). To put `<rapi-doc>` on a page of your own app, you don't need one: see [Framework Integration](/docs/integrations/).

All integrations follow one contract, so they take the same options, serve the same routes and send the same HTML. This page describes it.

## What an integration does

1. **Takes the standard options** (below), under the names its language prefers.
2. **Serves the routes**: the docs page, the OAuth return page and, unless the bundle comes from a CDN, `rapidoc-min.js` with its license file.
3. **Finds the spec**: defaults `specUrl` to the framework's own OpenAPI endpoint, for example `/openapi.json` in FastAPI or `/v3/api-docs` with springdoc.
4. **Ships one `rapidoc` release**: the bundle, its license file and `integration.json`, embedded in the integration's package.

## Options

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `uiPath` | `/docs` | URL path the docs page is served at, including any prefix the app is mounted under. Contract version 1 called it `path`, which is still read. |
| `specUrl` | the framework's endpoint | URL of the OpenAPI document. |
| `spec` | | The OpenAPI document itself, written into the page. |
| `title` | `API Reference` | Page title. |
| `assets` | `bundled` | `bundled`: the integration serves the bundle. `cdn`: jsDelivr, at the pinned version with its SRI hash. Or a URL of your own. |
| `options` | | [Attributes of `<rapi-doc>`](/docs/rapidoc/reference/), in kebab-case or camelCase. |
| `head`, `css` | | Markup and CSS added to the page as given. |
| `lang`, `nonce` | `en`, none | Page language; Content-Security-Policy nonce. |
| `enabled` | `true` | When false, the integration registers no routes. |

## In JavaScript

`@rapidoc/embed` implements the contract. An integration maps its routes to the framework:

```js
import { embedRoutes, renderHostPage, renderOAuthReceiverPage } from '@rapidoc/embed';
import { readAsset } from '@rapidoc/embed/node';

export function rapidoc(app, options) {
  for (const route of embedRoutes(options)) {
    app.get(route.path, (c) => {
      const body =
        route.kind === 'page' ? renderHostPage(options)
        : route.kind === 'oauth-receiver' ? renderOAuthReceiverPage(options)
        : readAsset(route.file);
      return c.body(body, 200, { 'content-type': route.contentType });
    });
  }
}
```

`@rapidoc/hono` is the reference integration for JavaScript server frameworks: about 80 lines over these functions, with a second entry for runtimes without a file system.

A documentation-site plugin is a different shape: the site has its own layout, bundler and sidebar, so there is no host page to serve. `@rapidoc/starlight` is the reference: it takes the same `uiPath`, `spec`, `title` and `options`, uses `toAttributes` for the element's attributes, imports the bundle through the site's bundler, and adds the operations to the site's sidebar.

In runtimes without a file system, use `assets: 'cdn'`: the page then loads the exact `rapidoc` version `@rapidoc/embed` depends on, checked against its SRI hash. A complete example on `node:http` is in the package (`examples/node-server.js`).

## In other languages

Port the reference implementation, `src/core.js` of `@rapidoc/embed`: about 150 lines of string functions with no imports. The package has the rules in words (`conformance/README.md`) and fixtures (`conformance/fixtures/`): each has an `input.json` and the expected HTML or route table. Your port conforms when its output equals every fixture, byte for byte for the pages.

The Python package `rapidoc` is the reference for other languages (the ASP.NET Core package, [`RapiDocContract.cs`](https://github.com/rapi-doc/RapiDoc/blob/master/integrations/rapidoc-dotnet/src/RapiDoc.AspNetCore/RapiDocContract.cs), is a second port, in a typed language, and [`contract.go`](https://github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go/blob/main/contract.go) of `rapidoc-go` a third, in a repository of its own with the fixtures copied in): its [`contract.py`](https://github.com/rapi-doc/RapiDoc/blob/master/integrations/rapidoc-python/src/rapidoc/contract.py) is the port, and its `setup_rapidoc()` shows the framework side: option names in the language's style, the framework's own OpenAPI URL as the default, and its path-prefix setting (`root_path`) in the page's URLs.

## Files `rapidoc` publishes for integrations

Every `rapidoc` release has these in `dist/`, next to the bundles:

| File | Import | Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `integration.json` | `rapidoc/integration.json` | Version, CDN base URL, and each file's role, content type, size and SRI hash. |
| `rapidoc-options.schema.json` | `rapidoc/options.schema.json` | JSON Schema of every attribute: validate configuration, or generate typed options in your language. |
| `custom-elements.json` | `rapidoc/custom-elements.json` | [Custom Elements Manifest](https://github.com/webcomponents/custom-elements-manifest): attributes, events, slots and methods for editors and tooling. |
| `rapidoc.d.ts`, `flow.d.ts`, `react.d.ts`, `vue.d.ts` | `rapidoc`, `rapidoc/flow`, `rapidoc/react`, `rapidoc/vue` | TypeScript types of the elements and their attributes. |
| `oauth-receiver.html` | | The OAuth return page, for serving next to `rapidoc-min.js`. |

## Checklist

- The docs page works at `uiPath` with and without a trailing slash, and under a path prefix or reverse proxy.
- `rapidoc-min.js.LICENSE.txt` is served or shipped wherever the bundle is.
- The OAuth return page is on the same origin as the docs page.
- With a Content-Security-Policy, the page gets a `nonce` and the policy allows the script's origin.
- The integration states which `rapidoc` version it ships, and passes the fixtures of the contract version it implements.
- Add the keyword `rapidoc-integration` and start the description with "RapiDoc for …", so the package is listed with the others. `@rapidoc/<host>` on npm and `rapidoc` on other registries are the official packages; a community package uses its own scope or name.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/build-your-own/

---

# Documentation Sites

> Add RapiDoc API reference pages to a Starlight, VitePress or Docusaurus site, with the API's operations in the site's sidebar.

## Starlight

`@rapidoc/starlight` adds an API reference page per OpenAPI document to a [Starlight](https://starlight.astro.build) site. The page uses Starlight's layout and themes, and the API's operations appear in Starlight's sidebar.

```bash
npm install @rapidoc/starlight
```

```javascript title="astro.config.mjs"
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config';
import starlight from '@astrojs/starlight';
import starlightRapidoc from '@rapidoc/starlight';

export default defineConfig({
  integrations: [
    starlight({
      title: 'My docs',
      plugins: [starlightRapidoc({ uiPath: '/docs/rapidoc/reference/', spec: './openapi.yaml' })],
    }),
  ],
});
```

`spec` is a file, a URL or an object, read when the site is built. For several APIs pass `{ apis: [...] }`.

## VitePress

VitePress has no plugin system, so there are two steps: wrap the config, and put the component on a page.

```javascript title=".vitepress/config.mjs"
import { defineConfig } from 'vitepress';
import { withRapidoc, rapidocSidebar } from '@rapidoc/vitepress';

export default withRapidoc(
  defineConfig({
    themeConfig: {
      sidebar: [{ text: 'Pets API', items: await rapidocSidebar({ spec: './openapi.yaml', uiPath: '/docs/rapidoc/reference/' }) }],
    },
  }),
  { apis: { pets: './openapi.yaml' } },
);
```

```md title="api.md"
---
layout: page
---

<script setup>
import { RapidocReference } from '@rapidoc/vitepress/client';
</script>

<RapidocReference api="pets" />
```

## Docusaurus

Three steps: the plugin, a doc page, and the sidebar.

```javascript title="docusaurus.config.js"
export default {
  plugins: [['@rapidoc/docusaurus', { apis: { pets: './openapi.yaml' } }]],
};
```

```mdx title="docs/api.mdx"
---
hide_table_of_contents: true
---

import RapidocReference from '@rapidoc/docusaurus/client';

<RapidocReference api="pets" />
```

```javascript title="sidebars.js"
import { rapidocSidebarSync } from '@rapidoc/docusaurus';

export default {
  docs: [
    {
      type: 'category',
      label: 'Pets API',
      items: rapidocSidebarSync({ spec: './openapi.yaml', uiPath: '/docs/api', docId: 'api' }),
    },
  ],
};
```

For another framework or site generator, see [Build an Integration](/docs/integrations/build-your-own/).

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/docs-sites/

---

# ASP.NET Core

> Serve a RapiDoc API reference from an ASP.NET Core app with the RapiDoc.AspNetCore NuGet package.

```bash
dotnet add package RapiDoc.AspNetCore
```

```csharp
using RapiDoc.AspNetCore;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapOpenApi();
app.MapRapiDoc(options => options.Attributes["render-style"] = "focused");

app.Run();
```

The reference is at `/docs` and reads the document `MapOpenApi()` serves at `/openapi/v1.json`. With Swashbuckle or NSwag, set `options.SpecUrl` to their document. `MapRapiDoc` returns an endpoint builder, so `.RequireAuthorization()` protects the reference, and `MapRapiDoc("/reference")` moves it. Needs .NET 8 or later.

The package and its options are described in its [README](https://github.com/rapi-doc/RapiDoc/tree/master/integrations/rapidoc-dotnet#readme).

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/dotnet/

---

# Front-End Frameworks

> Use <rapi-doc>, <rapi-doc-mini> and <rapi-flow> in React, Next.js, Vue, Nuxt, Angular, Svelte and Astro, with types for their attributes.

`<rapi-doc>` is a standard custom element, so it works in any framework without a wrapper. Two rules apply everywhere:

- **Register it in the browser.** `import 'rapidoc'` defines the element and needs `window`, so with server-side rendering import it on the client only.
- **Pass attributes as strings**, as in HTML: `render-style="view"`, `allow-try="false"`.

## React and Next.js

Import RapiDoc in an effect, so it runs only in the browser. In the Next.js App Router, mark the file `'use client'`.

```tsx title="ApiDocs.tsx"
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';

export default function ApiDocs() {
  useEffect(() => {
    import('rapidoc');
  }, []);

  return (
    <rapi-doc
      spec-url="https://rapidocui.com/specs/petstore.yaml"
      render-style="view"
      show-header="false"
      style={{ height: '100vh' }}
    />
  );
}
```

The element renders once it is defined; until then the browser shows it as an empty box.

### TypeScript

TypeScript doesn't know `<rapi-doc>` and reports `Property 'rapi-doc' does not exist on type 'JSX.IntrinsicElements'`. `rapidoc` ships the types; reference them once, for example in `src/rapidoc.d.ts`:

```typescript title="src/rapidoc.d.ts"
/// <reference types="rapidoc/react" />
```

Every attribute is then checked and completed in JSX: `render-style="nope"` is an error. For a typed ref, import the element's type:

```tsx
import type { RapiDocElement } from 'rapidoc';

const ref = useRef<RapiDocElement>(null);
// ref.current?.loadSpec('/openapi.json');
```

The types need `rapidoc` 12.2 or later. `<rapi-doc-mini>` and `<rapi-flow>` are typed from 12.2.1.

## Vue and Nuxt

Tell the Vue compiler that tags starting with `rapi-` are custom elements, not missing Vue components:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="vite.config.js">
```javascript
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import vue from '@vitejs/plugin-vue';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    vue({
      template: {
        compilerOptions: {
          isCustomElement: (tag) => tag.startsWith('rapi-'),
        },
      },
    }),
  ],
});
```
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="nuxt.config.ts">
```typescript
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  vue: {
    compilerOptions: {
      isCustomElement: (tag) => tag.startsWith('rapi-'),
    },
  },
});
```
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

For attribute checking in templates (with Volar), add the types once, for example in `src/rapidoc.d.ts`:

```typescript title="src/rapidoc.d.ts"
/// <reference types="rapidoc/vue" />
```

Then import RapiDoc when the component mounts:

```vue title="ApiDocs.vue"
<script setup>
import { onMounted } from 'vue';

onMounted(() => import('rapidoc'));
</script>

<template>
  <rapi-doc
    spec-url="https://rapidocui.com/specs/petstore.yaml"
    render-style="focused"
    style="height: 100vh"
  ></rapi-doc>
</template>
```

## Angular

Add `CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA` to the component (or its module) and import RapiDoc:

```typescript title="api-docs.component.ts"
import { Component, CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA } from '@angular/core';
import 'rapidoc';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-api-docs',
  standalone: true,
  schemas: [CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA],
  template: `
    <rapi-doc
      spec-url="https://rapidocui.com/specs/petstore.yaml"
      render-style="view"
      style="height: 100vh"
    ></rapi-doc>
  `,
})
export class ApiDocsComponent {}
```

With Angular SSR, move the import into `afterNextRender` so it runs in the browser only.

## Svelte, Astro and plain bundlers

No configuration is needed. Import `rapidoc` in a client-side script and use the element in your markup. In Astro, a `<script>import 'rapidoc';</script>` tag in the page is enough.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/front-end/

---

# Go

> Serve a RapiDoc API reference from a Go app with github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go, a net/http handler with no dependencies.

```bash
go get github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go
```

```go
import rapidoc "github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go"

mux := http.NewServeMux()

docs := rapidoc.Handler(rapidoc.Options{
	SpecURL:    "/openapi.json",
	Attributes: map[string]any{"render-style": "focused"},
})
mux.Handle("/docs", docs)
mux.Handle("/docs/", docs)
```

The reference is at `/docs`. It is a plain `net/http` handler with no dependencies, so it also mounts on chi, Gin, Echo and Fiber, and next to [Huma](https://huma.rocks), whose `/openapi.json` it can read; the [README](https://github.com/rapi-doc/rapidoc-go#with-a-router-or-framework) has each of them. It does not generate the OpenAPI document: point `SpecURL` at the one your app serves, or pass the JSON as `Spec`. Needs Go 1.22 or later.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/go/

---

# Hono, Express & Fastify

> Serve a RapiDoc API reference from a Hono, Express or Fastify app with @rapidoc/hono, @rapidoc/express and @rapidoc/fastify.

A server can serve the API reference itself, next to the API. These packages add the page, the bundle and the OAuth return page to your app, so there is no HTML to write.

## Hono

```bash
npm install @rapidoc/hono
```

```javascript
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { rapidoc } from '@rapidoc/hono';

const app = new Hono();

app.get('/openapi.json', (c) => c.json(openApiDocument));
app.use(rapidoc({ specUrl: '/openapi.json', options: { renderStyle: 'focused' } }));
```

The reference is at `/docs`; change it with `uiPath`. `options` takes any [attribute of `<rapi-doc>`](/docs/rapidoc/reference/). On Cloudflare Workers, import from `@rapidoc/hono/edge`, which loads the bundle from a CDN instead of reading it from disk.

## Express and Fastify

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="Express">
```javascript
import express from 'express';
import { rapidoc } from '@rapidoc/express';

const app = express();

app.get('/openapi.json', (req, res) => res.json(openApiDocument));
app.use(rapidoc({ specUrl: '/openapi.json' }));
```
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Fastify">
```javascript
import Fastify from 'fastify';
import { rapidoc } from '@rapidoc/fastify';

const fastify = Fastify();

await fastify.register(rapidoc, { specUrl: '/openapi.json' });
```
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

Both serve the reference at `/docs` and take the same options as the Hono package. Mounted under a prefix (`app.use('/docs/rapidoc/reference/', …)`, or Fastify's `prefix`), the page's links include it.

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/node/

---

# FastAPI & Starlette

> Serve a RapiDoc API reference from a FastAPI or Starlette app with the rapidoc package from PyPI.

```bash
pip install rapidoc
```

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from rapidoc.fastapi import setup_rapidoc

app = FastAPI(docs_url=None, redoc_url=None)

setup_rapidoc(app, options={"render_style": "focused"})
```

The reference is at `/docs` and reads the app's own `/openapi.json`. `docs_url=None` turns off FastAPI's Swagger UI, which uses the same path; to keep both, pass `ui_path="/reference"`. For a plain Starlette app, import it from `rapidoc.starlette` and pass `spec_url`.

The package, its options and the Starlette setup are described in its [README](https://github.com/rapi-doc/RapiDoc/tree/master/integrations/rapidoc-python#readme).

Source: https://rapidocui.com/docs/integrations/python/
